content: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are defined by difficulties in social interaction, communication challenges, and rigid patterns of thought and behavior. Acupuncture, a practice rooted in Traditional Chinese Medicine, involves the insertion of needles or application of pressure to specific points on the body. It has been increasingly adopted in Western medicine and has occasionally been used as a treatment to address symptoms of ASD. However, its clinical efficacy and safety have not been thoroughly evaluated. The objective of this review was to assess whether acupuncture is effective in improving core symptoms of ASD, such as social and communication impairments, as well as secondary outcomes like cognitive function, overall functioning, and quality of life. Additionally, the review aimed to determine whether acupuncture is associated with any adverse effects. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to September 30, 2010, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and several Chinese-language databases. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials were included if they compared acupuncture with no treatment, placebo, or sham acupuncture in individuals with ASD. Studies comparing different forms of acupuncture or acupuncture with other treatments were excluded. Data from 10 trials involving 390 children with ASD, aged 3 to 18 years, were analyzed. The treatment durations ranged from four weeks to nine months. These studies were conducted in Hong Kong, mainland China, and Egypt. Two trials compared needle acupuncture with sham acupuncture and found no significant difference in core autistic features. However, there was some indication that needle acupuncture might improve secondary outcomes such as communication, cognitive function, and global functioning. Six trials compared needle acupuncture combined with conventional treatment to conventional treatment alone. Most of these trials did not demonstrate significant improvements in core autistic features. However, one trial reported that children in the acupuncture group were more likely to show improvement on the Autism Behavior Checklist and had slightly better post-treatment scores. There was no strong evidence that acupuncture improved communication or linguistic abilities, though some benefits were observed for cognitive function and global functioning. Two trials evaluated acupressure combined with conventional treatment versus conventional treatment alone. These studies did not report on core autistic features but suggested potential benefits for secondary outcomes like communication, cognitive function, and global functioning. Adverse effects were reported in four trials, though detailed quantitative data were limited. Both intervention and control groups experienced adverse effects, which included bleeding, crying due to fear or pain, irritability, sleep disturbances, and increased hyperactivity. None of the trials assessed quality of life as an outcome. The evidence base has several limitations. The trials were few in number and exclusively involved children, with no studies conducted on adults. Six of the trials were at high risk of bias, and there was significant variability in participant characteristics, interventions, and outcome measures. The studies were of short duration, lacked long-term follow-up, and produced inconsistent and imprecise results. Additionally, the large number of analyses conducted increased the risk of false-positive findings. In conclusion, current evidence does not support the use of acupuncture as a treatment for ASD. There is no definitive evidence that acupuncture is effective for managing ASD symptoms in children, and no randomized controlled trials have been conducted in adults. Further high-quality, large-scale trials with longer follow-up periods are necessary to establish the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for ASD.
